passages.title: Beyond the Tragedy
passages.text:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay with a memorable title, "The Tragedy of the Commons." Imagine, he wrote, a pasture open to every herder in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal to the pasture but bears only a small share of the damage that the extra grazing does. Reasoning this way, every herder adds animals, and the pasture is ruined. Hardin himself called for "mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon," but his essay was widely read as showing that shared resources would be destroyed unless they were either divided into private property or placed under the control of a government.

The argument was elegant, and it spread quickly. It seemed to explain overfished seas, polluted rivers, and exhausted groundwater. For years many economists treated the tragedy less as a hypothesis to be tested than as a law to be applied.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom was not satisfied. Rather than reasoning about an imagined pasture, she went looking for real ones. With her colleagues, she gathered hundreds of case studies of fisheries, forests, irrigation systems, and grazing lands that communities had shared for long periods. In a Swiss mountain village, farmers had grazed cattle on common summer pastures for centuries under rules that limited how many animals each family could send up the mountain. In parts of Spain, farmers had shared water from irrigation canals for generations, taking turns according to schedules that everyone could see and that neighbors enforced on one another. Elected water judges heard complaints at regular public meetings, and a farmer caught taking water out of turn paid a fine set by people who knew the canal as well as the farmer did. Similar arrangements turned up in fishing villages, in forests held by villages in Japan, and in shared grazing lands elsewhere.

Ostrom did not claim that every commons succeeds. Many of her cases ended in collapse, just as Hardin predicted. Her point was that collapse is not inevitable. What distinguished the lasting cases, she argued, was not private ownership or outside control but a set of arrangements the users had worked out themselves. The boundaries of the resource and the list of people entitled to use it were clear. The people bound by the rules had a voice in changing them. Users monitored one another, and penalties for breaking the rules were graduated: a first offense might bring a small fine or a public warning, while repeated offenses brought heavier ones. Disputes could be settled quickly and cheaply, often by the users themselves.

Some of her findings ran against common sense. Rules imposed by distant authorities, however well designed, often worked worse than rougher rules that users had made, partly because outsiders could not watch every field and canal, and partly because people who had no say in a rule had less reason to respect it. In several cases, a government that took over a well-run commons with good intentions destroyed the very cooperation it meant to protect.

In 2009 Ostrom became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in economics. Her work did not prove Hardin wrong so much as show that he had described one possible ending as if it were the only one. The herders in his story never speak to one another. Ostrom's herders do, and that difference turns out to matter a great deal.

passages.title: The Island in the City
passages.text:
On a still summer evening, a thermometer in the center of a large city may read several degrees higher than one in the farmland a few miles away. The difference is not a quirk of a single instrument. Measured across many cities and many years, the pattern is consistent enough to have a name, the urban heat island, and it is usually strongest not in the afternoon, when the sun is high, but after dark. In a large city on a calm, clear night, the gap between downtown and the surrounding countryside can be considerably larger than it is at midday, and it tends to shrink when clouds or a strong wind move in.

That timing is a clue to the cause. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them and store the energy as heat. A field of grass or a stand of trees absorbs sunlight too, but plants also release water vapor through their leaves, and turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air. A city has replaced much of that cooling vegetation with materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by trapping some of the heat that the streets radiate upward, and engines, air conditioners, and furnaces add heat of their own.

The consequences are not evenly shared. Within a single city, temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next, and the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement. Because heat that lingers into the night denies the body a chance to recover, these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave, especially for older residents and for people without air conditioning.

One response has been to make surfaces reflect more sunlight. A roof coated in a pale, reflective material can stay far cooler on a sunny afternoon than a dark one, and some cities now require or encourage such roofs on new buildings. The idea is simple, but its effects depend on circumstances. In a place with hot summers and mild winters, a reflective roof saves energy that would have gone to cooling. In a place with long, cold winters, the same roof also reflects sunlight that would have helped warm the building, and part of the summer savings may be lost.

Trees offer a different kind of help. A street tree shades the pavement beneath it, so less sunlight is stored in the first place, and it cools the air through its leaves. Unlike a coating, though, a tree takes years to grow, needs water and room for its roots, and can be lost to drought or disease. Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees. Many cities now try to do both.

Researchers continue to argue about how much each measure can accomplish, and the answer clearly varies from city to city. What is no longer in dispute is the basic picture: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it, which means that it can also be changed by the choices made in rebuilding it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Proof
passages.text:
My aunt Lena opened the bakery at four every morning, and that summer I opened it with her. I had asked for the job because I wanted money for a used guitar, and she had agreed because, as she told my mother on the phone, it would be good for me to see what four in the morning looked like. I did not yet know that she meant this as a kindness.

The first week, she let me do almost nothing. I swept flour from the corners, carried trays, and watched her hands. She worked the dough without hurrying, folding it over itself, pressing it down with the heel of her palm, turning it a quarter turn, and folding again. When I asked how she knew when it was ready, she said, "It tells you," and kept folding. I took this for the kind of thing adults say when they do not want to explain.

In the second week she gave me a bowl of my own. I folded and pressed and turned exactly as I had seen her do, and my dough stayed sticky and slack. I worked faster. It got worse. Lena glanced over once, said nothing, and went back to her ovens. By six the first customers were lined up outside, and my bowl sat on the back counter under a damp towel like something I hoped nobody would ask about.

I remember being furious, though not at her. I was furious at the dough, which seemed to have decided against me, and at myself for having believed that watching was the same as knowing. My father, who builds cabinets, once told me that the first hundred drawers a carpenter makes are practice for the next hundred. I had always heard this as a joke about patience. That morning it sounded more like a warning.

On the third Monday I came in early, before Lena, and let myself in with the key she had given me without comment the week before. I mixed a batch and, instead of copying her hands, paid attention to my own. I noticed when the dough fought me and when it gave, how it went from tacky to smooth against my palm, how it began, after a while, to push back. I did not hurry. When Lena arrived she hung up her coat, tied on her apron, and stood beside me for what felt like a long time.

"Again," she said. I folded it again. "There," she said, and walked off to light the ovens.

That was all. She did not tell me it was good, and I understood, standing there with flour to my elbows, that she was not going to. What she had given me instead was the key, the early mornings, and a bowl of my own to ruin. I had spent two weeks waiting for her to explain something that could not be explained, only noticed. The loaves from my batch went into the case at seven, unmarked among hers, and I watched a woman in a green coat buy one without looking twice.

I bought the guitar in August. I still play it, badly, most evenings. But when people ask what I learned that summer, I do not tell them about bread. I tell them that some things wait to be noticed, and that the people who know them best are often the ones who say the least about them.

questions.evidence: My concern is with treating daylighting as a symbol rather than a tool.
questions.stem: In Passage B, the author's central concern about daylighting is that it:

choices.A: always costs more than repairing the existing pipes.
choices.B: may be chosen for its appeal rather than for how well it manages water.
choices.C: inevitably harms the wildlife it is meant to support.
choices.D: is unpopular with the residents of the neighborhoods involved.

questions.explanation: The author states the concern directly: daylighting should not be treated "as a symbol rather than a tool." A city should first ask how best to manage the water, and sometimes the answer is not a stream.

hints: Look for the sentence in which the author names a concern directly.

strategy.explanation: The last paragraph states the concern; eliminate the extreme choices.

questions.subskill: Central idea of an informational passage
questions.evidence: In effect, the plant has separated two tasks that most plants perform together: gathering carbon at night and using it by day.
questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: describing how botanists first discovered CAM in the stonecrop family.
choices.B: explaining how some desert plants limit water loss and noting the costs of that strategy.
choices.C: arguing that cacti use water more efficiently than any other kind of plant.
choices.D: comparing how desert plants and meadow plants absorb water from the soil.

questions.explanation: Most of the passage explains how CAM plants take in carbon at night to save water (paragraphs 1–4), then describes the strategy's cost (paragraph 5) and draws a general lesson (paragraph 6). B covers both the mechanism and its cost.

distractor_explanations.A: The stonecrop family is mentioned only to explain the name; the discovery itself is not described.
distractor_explanations.C: The passage never claims cacti are the most efficient of all plants.
distractor_explanations.D: Meadow plants appear only in one comparison about growth rate, and soil absorption is not discussed.

hints: Which choice accounts for both the mechanism and its drawback?

strategy.explanation: Summarize: 'CAM saves water but slows growth,' then match.

questions.remember: Main idea covers the passage's whole arc.

questions.evidence: When the sun rises, the stomata close, sealing the plant against the heat.
questions.stem: According to the passage, CAM plants keep their stomata closed during the day mainly in order to:

choices.A: reduce the amount of water they lose in the heat.
choices.B: store carbon dioxide inside their cells as an acid.
choices.C: absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis.
choices.D: release carbon dioxide they took in overnight.

questions.subskill: Points of agreement across paired passages
questions.evidence: Where a buried stream runs beneath an open lot or a park, the costs can be modest and the benefits real.
questions.stem: The authors of both passages would most likely agree that:

choices.A: daylighting is usually the most effective way for a city to manage storm water.
choices.B: restored streams tend to support wildlife soon after they are first opened.
choices.C: cities should generally spend less on repairing their storm-water pipes.
choices.D: daylighting can be worthwhile in some places but very costly in others.

questions.explanation: Passage A says daylighting "is not cheap" and can be "prohibitive" where buildings sit above a stream, while arguing that it brings real benefits. Passage B says costs can be many times higher in dense neighborhoods but "modest" near open lots, where the benefits are "real." Both accept that it can be worthwhile in some places and very costly in others.

distractor_explanations.A: Passage B explicitly doubts this, suggesting rain gardens and permeable pavement may be more effective in many cases.
distractor_explanations.B: Passage B says some channels need years of maintenance before supporting wildlife.
distractor_explanations.C: Neither author argues for abandoning pipe repair; Passage B treats repair as a cheaper option.

hints: Find what each passage says about cost.
Does either passage say daylighting can be worthwhile in some cases?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate any choice that one author would reject; the survivor must fit both.

questions.remember: Agreement questions: the answer must fit both authors.

questions.subskill: Predicting one author's response to the other
questions.evidence: For the same budget, a city might install rain gardens and permeable pavement across dozens of blocks, capturing storm water closer to where it falls.
questions.stem: Based on Passage B, how would its author most likely respond to Passage A's claim that a restored stream "can spread that water out and slow it down"?

choices.A: By questioning whether a restored stream can slow down storm water at all
choices.B: By suggesting that other methods might manage the water at a lower cost
choices.C: By agreeing that daylighting should be a city's first choice for flood control
choices.D: By arguing that flooding is rarely a serious problem for most cities

questions.explanation: Passage B does not dispute that streams can manage water; it questions whether daylighting is the most effective use of the money, pointing to rain gardens and permeable pavement that capture water across many blocks.

distractor_explanations.C: Passage B says the first question should be about the most effective way to manage water, not about bringing the stream back.
distractor_explanations.D: Passage B treats storm-water management as a serious goal; it does not dismiss flooding.

hints: Does Passage B dispute what streams can do, or something else?

strategy.explanation: Find Passage B's alternative to daylighting and connect it to the flood claim.

questions.remember: A critic often concedes the point and questions the priority.

questions.evidence: masting should be most pronounced in species whose seeds are eaten by specialists
questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, masting would be expected to be LEAST pronounced in a tree species whose seeds are eaten mainly by:

choices.A: weevils that feed almost entirely on that species' seeds.
choices.B: squirrels whose numbers rise and fall with the size of the crop.
choices.C: animals that also eat many other kinds of food.
choices.D: a beetle that lays its eggs only inside those seeds.

questions.explanation: Predator satiation works by starving down predators that depend on one food. Animals with many other foods are not starved down in lean years, so masting would help least and be least pronounced.

distractor_explanations.A: Weevils that rely on one food are specialists, where masting should be most pronounced.
distractor_explanations.B: Predators that track the crop are the ones masting is said to starve down.
distractor_explanations.D: A beetle that uses only those seeds is a specialist.

hints: The passage says where masting is MOST pronounced. What is the opposite case?

strategy.explanation: Note the word LEAST, then reverse the passage's prediction.

questions.remember: For LEAST/EXCEPT questions, find the rule and take its opposite.

questions.evidence: would waste much of the effort
questions.stem: According to paragraph 4, a tree that flowered heavily in a year when its neighbors did not would most likely:

choices.C: produce more seeds than usual, since it would face less competition for pollen.

questions.remember: The main focus of a narrative covers its central discovery and its resolution.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main claim of the passage?
